lessons.title: Lesson 1: What the skilled trades are
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe seven common trades and pick two that fit you.
This lesson builds toward: Given seven common trades and your own interests and limits, you will describe what each trade does and choose two that fit you, with one reason for each choice.
Electricians install and repair wiring, lights and power in homes and buildings. Plumbers install and fix pipes, water heaters and drains. HVAC technicians work on heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration. Welders join metal with heat for buildings, ships, pipelines and factories.
Solar installers put solar panels on roofs and on the ground and connect them. Carpenters build and repair frames, floors, stairs and cabinets. CDL truck drivers move goods across town or across the country with a commercial driver's license.
Think about what fits you. Do you like working outside or inside? High up, or on the ground? Do you like math and figuring out problems? Can you be away from home for days, as long-haul drivers often are? Do you like fixing things for customers or building new things? Your answers point to a trade.
Many skills carry over. Military mechanics and logistics, sports discipline and teamwork, and work or training programs done while incarcerated (maintenance, kitchen, building trades) all count.
Words to know:
- Skilled trade: a job that needs special hands-on training, such as electrician or welder.
- HVAC: heating, ventilation and air conditioning.
- CDL: commercial driver's license, needed to drive large trucks and buses.
Try it now: Answer the "What fits you?" questions in writing. Then pick the two trades that match your answers best and write one sentence for each saying why.
You can now describe common skilled trades and pick two that fit how you like to work.

check.q: What does an electrician mainly work on?
check.why: Electricians install and fix wiring, power and lighting.

check.q: You like solving problems, do not mind tight spaces and want local work. How would you choose?
options: Pick the trade a friend chose
Pick the one with the coolest name
Compare trades against your answers and pick two that fit
Pick long-haul trucking because it pays
check.why: Matching trades to your own interests and limits gives the best fit.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Checking pay and training on official sites
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Look up a trade's pay, training and job outlook in the Occupational Outlook Handbook.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh, you will look up a trade's median pay, usual training, license needs and job outlook, with the year of the pay figure written down.
Do not trust pay numbers from ads or social media. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh. It is free and is updated regularly.
Each job has a profile with tabs. "Pay" shows the median pay, meaning half of workers earn more and half earn less. "How to Become One" shows the training, such as an apprenticeship, and whether a license is needed. "Job Outlook" shows whether the number of jobs is expected to grow. "State and Area Data" shows pay where you live.
For example, the electricians profile says most electricians learn in a 4- or 5-year apprenticeship, and most states require electricians to be licensed. Starting pay as an apprentice is lower than the median and usually rises as you gain skills.
AI assistants can help explain the words on these pages, but take the numbers from the official page, not from the AI.
Step by step:
- Go to bls.gov/ooh.
- Search for the trade, for example "electricians" or "plumbers".
- Open the profile and read the Pay tab: write down the median pay and the year.
- Read How to Become One: write down the training and license.
- Read Job Outlook and State and Area Data.
Words to know:
- Median pay: the middle pay: half of workers earn more and half earn less.
- Job outlook: whether the number of jobs in a field is expected to grow or shrink.
- BLS: the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the government office that collects job and pay data.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook
- Occupational Outlook Handbook: Electricians
Try it now: Look up your two trades from Lesson 1 on bls.gov/ooh. For each, write the median pay and the year it is for, the usual training, whether a license is needed, and the job outlook.
You can now find a trade's real median pay, training path and job outlook on the official handbook.

check.q: What does job outlook tell you?
options: How fast jobs in the trade are expected to grow
check.why: Job outlook shows whether the number of jobs is expected to grow or shrink.

check.q: A video says plumbers all earn a very high amount. What would you do?
options: Believe it because it is popular
Check the median pay and its year on bls.gov/ooh
check.why: Official pay data on bls.gov/ooh is the place to check.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Apprenticeships, pre-apprenticeships and licenses
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain how apprenticeships, pre-apprenticeships and licenses work for your trade.
This lesson builds toward: For your top trade, you will explain how its apprenticeship, pre-apprenticeship and license or certification work, with the official state board page found.
A Registered Apprenticeship is a paid job with training. The US Department of Labor's apprenticeship.gov says apprentices get paid work experience with a mentor, a wage that goes up as their skills grow, and a nationally recognized credential at the end. You learn on the job and in classes.
A pre-apprenticeship gets you ready to enter an apprenticeship. It can last a few weeks to a few months and may or may not pay. It often covers basic math, tool use, safety, and job readiness, and it can help you get accepted. Many reentry programs and community colleges run them.
Licenses and certificates differ by trade and state. Electricians and plumbers usually need a state or local license after their training. HVAC technicians who handle refrigerants must have EPA Section 608 certification. New truck drivers must finish entry-level driver training with a provider on the federal Training Provider Registry before taking the CDL tests. Welders and solar installers often earn industry certifications that employers ask for.
Veterans: the VA says GI Bill benefits can be used for many apprenticeships and on-the-job training, and Helmets to Hardhats connects veterans with construction apprenticeships.
Words to know:
- Registered Apprenticeship: a paid job with training, approved by the Department of Labor or a state, that ends with a recognized credential.
- Pre-apprenticeship: a short program that prepares you to get into an apprenticeship.
- License: official permission from a state or city to do certain work, such as electrical work.
- Certification: proof that you passed a test or training for a skill.
Official sources:
- Apprenticeship.gov: Career seekers
- Apprenticeship.gov: What is a pre-apprenticeship?
- EPA: Section 608 technician certification
- FMCSA Training Provider Registry: who needs entry-level driver training
- VA: On-the-job training and apprenticeships
Try it now: For your top trade, write down: is it usually learned through an apprenticeship? What license or certification does it need? Then search "[your state] [trade] license" and find the official state board page (look for an address ending in .gov).
You can now explain how apprenticeships, pre-apprenticeships and licenses work and find your state's license page.

check.q: How is an apprenticeship different from a regular class?
options: You do not learn any skills
You work and earn a wage while you learn
It never leads to a credential
check.why: Apprentices are paid to work while they learn the trade.

check.q: You want to know what license your trade needs in your state. What would you do?
options: Find the official state board page ending in .gov
Ask a random social media group
Buy the first online course you see
check.why: The state board's official page has the real license rules.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Getting in and staying safe

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Tools and safety on the job
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the basic safety gear and habits every trade expects.
This lesson builds toward: For your top trade, you will list the safety gear, safety habits and basic tools the work needs, checked against a program's official tool list.
Every trade expects you to work safely from day one. Common personal protective equipment (PPE) includes safety glasses, a hard hat, gloves, steel-toe or safety-toe boots, hearing protection and high-visibility vests. Welders also need a welding helmet and flame-resistant clothing. Workers on roofs need fall protection.
Basic habits: inspect your tools before use; keep your area clean; never remove a guard from a machine; use the right ladder and keep three points of contact; and lift with your legs, not your back. Electricians and maintenance workers must follow lockout/tagout rules, which keep machines and power off while someone works on them.
Many employers and unions ask new workers to take an OSHA 10-hour safety course. It is a training card, not a license, but it shows you know the basics.
Your employer must provide required safety gear and training. Ask your program which tools you must buy yourself; apprentices often start with a small set of hand tools, such as a tape measure, a utility knife, pliers, screwdrivers and a tool bag.
Step by step:
- Wear the PPE the job requires before you start.
- Inspect tools and cords for damage.
- Keep guards on machines and the work area clean.
- Use ladders with three points of contact.
- Ask before you do anything you were not trained to do.
Words to know:
- PPE: personal protective equipment: gear like glasses, gloves and hard hats that protects you.
- Lockout/tagout: steps that keep a machine or power switched off and locked while someone works on it.
- OSHA 10: a 10-hour basic safety training course for workers, with a completion card.
Try it now: For your top trade, list the PPE you would wear and five hand tools you would likely need. Then ask a program near you, or check its website, for its official tool list.
You can now name the safety gear and habits your trade expects and prepare a starter tool list.

check.q: Which is a basic safety habit in the trades?
options: Wearing the right PPE for the task
Working on live power to save time
check.why: Wearing the right PPE protects you from common hazards.

check.q: Your program sends a starter tool list, but a store suggests an expensive kit. What would you do?
options: Follow the program's official tool list
check.why: The program's list tells you what you actually need.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Second-chance options if you have a record
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find second-chance programs and incentives and plan how to handle a record in the trades.
This lesson builds toward: If you or someone you help has a record, you will find second-chance programs and plan questions for the licensing board, naming the Federal Bonding Program and the Work Opportunity Tax Credit.
A record does not have to block a trades career. Many apprenticeship programs, unions and employers hire people with records, and many reentry organizations run pre-apprenticeship programs aimed at people coming home.
Two federal tools help employers say yes. The Federal Bonding Program can give the employer a free bond for the first six months of a job, at no cost to you or the employer, as the EEOC notes. The Work Opportunity Tax Credit gives employers a tax credit for hiring certain people, including a "qualified ex-felon" hired within a year of a felony conviction or release. The employer and the applicant complete IRS Form 8850 on or before the day of the job offer, so tell employers you may qualify.
Licenses and some jobs check records. Many state licensing boards look at records case by case. Before you spend money on training, contact the board for your trade and ask how they review records. Some CDL endorsements, such as hazardous materials, need a federal background check.
Ask a legal aid office or your reentry program whether your record can be sealed or expunged in your state, and practice a short, honest answer about your record for interviews.
Step by step:
- Search for reentry or second-chance pre-apprenticeship programs near you.
- Ask employers if they use the Federal Bonding Program or the Work Opportunity Tax Credit.
- Contact your trade's state licensing board and ask how it reviews records.
- Ask legal aid about sealing or expungement.
- Practice a short, honest answer about your record.
Words to know:
- Federal Bonding Program: a free US Department of Labor program that insures employers for the first months when they hire people with records or other barriers.
- Work Opportunity Tax Credit: a federal tax credit employers can get for hiring people from certain groups, including some people with felony convictions.
- Licensing board: the state office that issues and reviews trade licenses.
Official sources:
- EEOC: Arrest and conviction records (mentions the Federal Bonding Program)
- IRS: Work Opportunity Tax Credit
- US Department of Labor: Work Opportunity Tax Credit
Try it now: Write three questions to ask your trade's state licensing board about how it reviews records. Then write two sentences you could say to an employer about the Federal Bonding Program and the Work Opportunity Tax Credit. (If you do not have a record, do this for a friend or as practice.)
You can now name second-chance tools for the trades and check how a licensing board reviews records before you pay for training.

check.q: What is the Work Opportunity Tax Credit?
options: A tax credit employers can get for hiring people from certain groups
check.why: WOTC gives employers a tax credit for hiring from certain groups, including some people with records.

check.q: You have a record and want a trade license. What would you do before paying for training?
options: Ask the state licensing board how it reviews records
Hide the record on the application
check.why: Many boards review records case by case, so ask first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Finding and applying to a program
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find two programs near you and make a plan to apply.
This lesson builds toward: Using apprenticeship.gov or a local job center, you will find two programs near you and write your first three steps to apply, with a date for each step and each program's application dates.
Start at apprenticeship.gov. Its Apprenticeship Job Finder lets you search by career and location and apply directly with the employer or program. If you cannot find a match, its Partner Finder shows organizations that accept new apprentice applications.
Other places to look: your local American Job Center (free job search help and sometimes training money), community colleges, union training centers for each trade, reentry programs, and veterans' programs.
Programs often ask for a high school diploma or GED, a valid ID, a driver's license for some trades, a basic math test, a drug test, and an interview. Find out the steps and the application dates, because some apprenticeships only take applications at certain times of year.
Get ready: brush up on basic math (fractions, measuring, simple algebra), get your documents together, and practice interview answers about safety, reliability and why you want the trade.
Step by step:
- Search apprenticeship.gov by trade and location.
- Write down two programs, their requirements and their application dates.
- Contact your local American Job Center or a union training center.
- Gather your documents: ID, diploma or GED, driver's license if needed.
- Practice basic math and your interview answers.
- Apply, and put the follow-up date on your calendar.
Words to know:
- American Job Center: a free government-funded office that helps people find jobs and training.
- GED: a test that gives you a high school equivalency credential.
- Union training center: a school run by a trade union and employers to train apprentices.
Official sources:
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Job Finder
- CareerOneStop: Find an American Job Center
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page Trade Start Plan. Include the trade, its median pay and outlook from bls.gov/ooh, the license or certification, two programs near you, your safety gear and starter tools, any second-chance resources, and your first three steps with dates.
You can now find apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship programs near you and make a dated plan to apply.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Trade and fit No clear trade, or no idea what the work is like. One trade with a short description of the work and why it fits. Compares it with a second trade and explains the choice. Pay and outlook Pay is missing, from an unofficial source, or has no year. Median pay with its year and the job outlook from bls.gov/ooh. Also notes the usual training from the handbook. License and programs License not checked, or fewer than two programs. The license or certification from the official state page and two programs near you. Includes each program's application dates and requirements. Safety gear and tools PPE or tools missing. Lists the PPE and starter tools for the trade. Checked against a program's official tool list. Second-chance resources Resources missing where they apply. Lists any second-chance resources that apply, or notes none apply. Includes questions for the licensing board and what to tell an employer. First three steps Steps are vague or have no dates. Three clear steps with dates. The first step is already done. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why write down each program's application dates?
options: Some programs only take applications at certain times
check.why: Missing an application window can mean waiting months.

check.q: A program near you has an entry test with measuring and fractions. What would you do?
options: Practice fractions, measuring and simple algebra before the test
check.why: Practicing the math ahead of time helps you pass entry tests.
